title: Symmetric STDP
intro: In the classical STDP window, the order of spikes decides the sign: pre-before-post strengthens and post-before-pre weakens. In a symmetric window, only the closeness in time matters. Spikes that land near each other in either order strengthen the synapse, so the rule detects synchrony and correlation rather than causation.

blocks.text: A convenient form is a narrow positive peak around zero with an optional wider negative surround, a "Mexican hat" in time:

blocks.source:
Delta w(Delta t) = A_plus exp(-|Delta t| / tau_plus) - A_minus' exp(-|Delta t| / tau_minus')
Delta t = t_post - t_pre;  tau_minus' > tau_plus, so near coincidences potentiate and loose ones depress

blocks.text: With no surround (A_minus' = 0), the rule potentiates every pairing and needs a separate mechanism, such as normalization or a decay term, to keep weights bounded. With a surround, uncorrelated spiking produces net depression, because random pairs at large |Delta t| fall in the negative wings more often than near the peak. Only inputs that are genuinely synchronized with the neuron grow.
The widget plots this window (in this library's simulator the surround has half the depression amplitude and three times the depression time constant) against the classical window for reference.

items: Set A- to 0. The window is all positive: every pairing potentiates, and you can see why a pure symmetric rule is unstable on its own.
Raise A- until the surround dips well below zero. The area under the curve becomes negative, so random, uncorrelated firing now weakens synapses, while coincident firing still strengthens them.
Narrow tau+ to 5 ms. The rule now only rewards near-exact synchrony.

Hippocampus. Mishra, Kim, Guzman and Jonas (2016) found a symmetric window at CA3-CA3 recurrent synapses in slices, where both orders potentiate over a broad window. That suits CA3's proposed role as an autoassociative memory: cells active together become wired together regardless of order, so a partial cue can recall the whole pattern.

Dopamine and neuromodulation. Brzosko, Schultz and Paulsen (2015) reported that in CA1, dopamine can convert post-before-pre depression into potentiation, giving an effectively symmetric window. The shape of STDP is not fixed but depends on neuromodulators, dendritic location and firing rate.

Theory. A symmetric Hebbian window is closely related to classical rate-based Hebb (dw ∝ x y): averaged over spike trains, it picks up the zero-lag correlation between pre- and postsynaptic activity, while an antisymmetric window picks up its temporal derivative, that is, sequence order.
Use symmetric STDP to learn which inputs belong together: assemblies, associative memories, the cells that represent the same object or feature.
Use classical (asymmetric) STDP to learn what predicts what: sequences, causal chains, latency reduction.

blocks.text: For a cortical column: both kinds of association appear in the Thousand Brains Theory. The output layer that represents an object (layer 2/3 in the 2017 columns paper) learns associations among cells that are active together while the same object is sensed. That is symmetric, order-free learning. The sequence and location layers need order, which is asymmetric. A practical design uses a symmetric rule with a negative surround for lateral connections within the object layer, and an asymmetric rule for connections that should learn to predict.

Sources: Mishra, R. K., Kim, S., Guzman, S. J. & Jonas, P. (2016), "Symmetric spike timing-dependent plasticity at CA3-CA3 synapses optimizes storage and recall in autoassociative networks", Nature Communications 7:11552. Brzosko, Z., Schultz, W. & Paulsen, O. (2015), "Retroactive modulation of spike timing-dependent plasticity by dopamine", eLife 4:e09685. Gerstner, W., Kistler, W. M., Naud, R. & Paninski, L. (2014), Neuronal Dynamics, Cambridge University Press, chapter 19. Hawkins, J., Ahmad, S. & Cui, Y. (2017), Frontiers in Neural Circuits 11:81.
